summary: States requirements for a standard SIP registration mechanism covering multiple addresses of record, suited to service providers supporting small and medium PBXs on a large scale, with at least E.164 phone number support. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: One office phone system has many numbers. This lists what is needed so a phone company can register them all at once.

what are the main requirements for pbx registration
how do phone numbers get registered in sip
subtitle: Requirements for SIP-PBXs to register multiple phone numbers with a service provider

tldr.problem: Small and medium office phone systems (SIP-PBXs) need to register hundreds of phone numbers with a service provider, but existing SIP methods are not standardized. Each provider uses different mechanisms, causing interoperability problems and requiring custom implementation for each vendor.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC states 20 requirements for a standardized SIP registration mechanism that allows a PBX to register multiple address-of-record (AOR) identifiers with a service provider in a scalable and interoperable way.
tldr.outcome: The requirements establish the foundation for solving fragmented SIP-PBX deployments and enable service providers to support PBXs on a large scale without proprietary extensions.

today: RFC 5947 is an Informational RFC stating requirements for SIP-PBX registration. It has not been obsoleted. The requirements guided the development of SIP mechanisms for multiple AOR registration, though not all requirements were addressed in a single protocol extension.

sections.title: The Problem with Multiple Phone Numbers
sections.content:
A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Private Branch Exchange (PBX) is an office phone system that handles many phone numbers. Unlike a single user registering with the network, a PBX typically controls tens or hundreds of phone numbers assigned by a service provider. When the PBX needs to receive calls for those numbers from outside, it must register its reachability information with the service provider.

In practice, SIP service providers and PBX vendors have developed proprietary solutions based on extensions to the SIP REGISTER method. These mechanisms vary in detail, causing interoperability problems. Some use P-Associated-URI headers listing all the AORs, some use wildcard syntax, and others use different routing strategies. This document describes the requirements for a standardized solution.
sections.plainLanguage: An office phone system has many phone numbers and needs to tell the phone company how to reach it for all of them, but different phone companies use different ways to do this.

sections.title: Specific Issues with Current Approaches
sections.content:
The problem manifests in three areas. First, REGISTER transactions may be mishandled by middleboxes that do not recognize implicit registrations, and the response can grow too large if listing hundreds of phone numbers. The wildcard syntax currently used violates TEL URI format rules.

Second, when the service provider routes inbound calls to the PBX, it is unclear which phone number was the intended target. The service provider may replace the Request-URI with the registered Contact URI, losing information about which number the call was for. Different providers place the target information in different header fields, creating inconsistency. Some providers expect the domain portion of the Contact URI to match the PBX's own identity rather than the service provider's domain.

Third, policy issues arise because service providers may check whether the calling identity (From or P-Asserted-Identity header) matches a registered AOR, but PBXs may change their Contact URI between transactions or use local domain names instead of the service provider's domain.
sections.plainLanguage: When registering many numbers, the response message gets too big, the receiving side does not know which number each call is for, and calling information does not match what was registered.

sections.title: Requirements for a Standardized Mechanism
sections.content:
The RFC specifies 20 requirements. The core requirements are that the mechanism MUST allow a PBX to register a set of assigned phone numbers (including E.164 numbers in ranges), allow the PBX to register reachability information, allow internal users to register for those numbers without involving the service provider, and allow the PBX to handle both internal calls and external calls from the service provider to those numbers.

A critical requirement is that the mechanism MUST provide a means for the PBX to know which assigned number an inbound request from the service provider is targeted at. Another essential requirement is backward compatibility: the mechanism MUST gracefully fail or fall back if one side does not support it, avoiding situations where one side believes the mechanism is in use while the other does not.

The mechanism MUST work over any SIP transport, support TLS and digest authentication, be compatible with existing intermediate network devices, work when the PBX has a dynamic IP address, and not require the PBX to publish a DNS name. Additional requirements allow extension to local numbers and arbitrary SIP URIs, provide support for GRUUs (globally routable user agent URIs), and include security guidance about authorization policies.
sections.plainLanguage: A good solution must allow the PBX and phone company to know which number each call is for, work even if one side upgrades first, handle dynamic IP addresses, and work with many kinds of intermediate network devices.

sections.title: Desirable Properties and Out-of-Scope Items
sections.content:
Beyond the core requirements, the document lists desirable properties. The mechanism SHOULD allow a service provider to reuse its existing mechanisms for handling normal user registrations to handle PBX registrations. It SHOULD scale to PBXs with several thousand assigned phone numbers. It SHOULD also scale to support thousands of PBXs on a single service provider.

Out of scope are third-party routing (how other domains route to the service provider for delivery to the PBX) and provisioning (how the service provider assigns numbers to the PBX and how the PBX learns those numbers). The focus is on the registration and call routing mechanisms, not the business process of assigning phone numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The solution should work with many phone numbers and many phone systems, and reuse existing technology when possible, but does not cover how phone numbers are assigned or how outside networks find the phone company.
